title: A Letter from Soren
notebook: Soren's reply: he signed the orders and authorized the operations. History will judge whether he was right.
Soren: my father was on his list as an organizer. He says he did not know him and did not hate him.
Soren will consider a public confession, only to complete the record. He says it is not an admission of guilt.

narrative.text: Soren's reply is written on heavy, cream-colored paper with his personal letterhead — the seal of the Veltrian General Staff, which he still uses despite being retired for fifteen years. The handwriting is precise, military, and unsettlingly calm.

I have been asked to read this to you. Soren writes: 'Chancellor. Your letter accused me of crimes. You are not wrong. I signed the orders. I authorized the operations. I did what I believed necessary to preserve the Veltrian state during a period of existential threat. History will judge whether I was right. Your father was among those I ordered executed. His name is on the list. I remember reviewing it. He was described as an organizer — a man who could have destabilized the government at a critical moment. I did not know him personally. I did not hate him. He was a threat, and I neutralized threats. That was my job. If you wish me to confess publicly, I will consider it — not as an admission of guilt, but as an acknowledgement that the historical record should be complete. You may contact my legal representative.'

choices.text: "He would confess. Not out of remorse — out of a desire for the historical record to be 'complete.' He killed my father and frames it as archival housekeeping. And yet — a confession is a confession. I will take it. I will not forgive it."
